title: Detrimental Effects of Irrelevant Speech on Serial Recall of Visual Items are Reflected in Reduced Visual N1 and Reduced Theta Activity
research_question: Does irrelevant speech, compared to continuous noise or silence, affect the neural processing of visually presented to-be-remembered items during a serial recall task, and do attentional aspects contribute to the Irrelevant Sound Effect (ISE)?

participants.description: 20 right-handed subjects (10 male; age 20-39 years) from Germany, unfamiliar with the specific design and hypotheses, reporting normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but likely university students given the authors' affiliations.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration, incomprehensible to subjects, amplitude normalized to RMS level of white noise), continuous white noise (power uniformly distributed between 0 and 22.05 kHz; 65 dB), or silence. Sounds were diotically presented via headphones.

Visual digits (1-9) presented successively in randomized order in the middle of the screen (112 pt Chicago font) for 700 ms each, with ISIs of 800-1000 ms. A warning stimulus (three decreasing rectangles) preceded digit presentation.

measures.instrument: Error rate (percentage of incorrectly recalled digits in sequence)
Visual N1 amplitude (156-176 ms), P1 amplitude (96-116 ms), P6 amplitude (580-600 ms)
Event-related spectral perturbations (ERSP) and spectral power changes (dB) during item presentation (400-800 ms post-stimulus onset) and silent retention phase

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during visual digit presentation
findings.mechanism: Interference with representations of to-be-remembered items in the phonological loop (Baddeley) or disruption of order information (Jones), or reduction of overall available attentional resources (Neath).
findings.quote: Strong performance deterioration under the speech condition for almost all serial positions (mean ± SE = 42 ± 1.9%) is shown

findings.antecedent: Continuous white noise during visual digit presentation
findings.mechanism: Steady-state sounds are encoded as a single object, not interfering with order information, or are easily ignored, not reducing attentional resources.
findings.quote: while the noise and silence conditions almost yield identical results (32 ± 1.5 and 31 ± 1.5% respectively).

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during visual digit presentation
findings.consequent: Visual N1 amplitude (156-176 ms) at posterior electrodes
findings.mechanism: Speech automatically captures attentional resources or impairs focusing attention on the visually presented item, leading to reduced processing of stimulus features in extrastriate occipito-parietal areas.
findings.quote: Two clusters of electrodes can be differentiated here, one posterior (less negativity for speech; Fig. 4, upper panel)

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during visual digit presentation
findings.consequent: Visual N1 amplitude (156-176 ms) at anterior electrodes
findings.mechanism: Speech automatically captures attentional resources or impairs focusing attention on the visually presented item, leading to reduced processing of stimulus features.
findings.quote: and one anterior (less positivity for speech; Fig. 4, lower panel). In both cases a left lateralized dominance appears to be present.

findings.antecedent: Continuous white noise during visual digit presentation
findings.mechanism: Continuous noise does not capture attentional resources in the same way as changing-state speech.
findings.quote: The effect clearly reflects a specific difference for speech. Two clusters of electrodes can be differentiated here, one posterior (less negativity for speech; Fig. 4, upper panel) and one anterior (less positivity for speech; Fig. 4, lower panel).

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during visual digit presentation (400-800 ms post-stimulus onset)
findings.consequent: Theta activity (4-6 Hz) at right prefrontal electrode (Fp2)
findings.mechanism: Reduced theta activity reflects reduced attentional resources directed to the to-be-remembered items, impairing working memory performance.
findings.quote: One right pre-frontal electrode (Fp2) showed a lower P-value than the one determined by the permutation test. The temporal evolution of theta activity for this electrode is displayed in the upper panel of Figure 5.

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during silent retention phase
findings.consequent: Theta power (4-6 Hz) at right prefrontal-frontotemporal electrodes
findings.mechanism: Reduced theta activity reflects reduced attentional resources or impaired working memory processes, which are crucial for retaining visual information.
findings.quote: This includes a cluster of right prefrontal-frontotemporal electrodes for the speech condition (left side of Fig. 6, top panel)

findings.antecedent: Continuous white noise during silent retention phase
findings.consequent: Theta power (4-6 Hz) at right prefrontal-frontotemporal electrodes (same cluster as speech effect)
findings.mechanism: Continuous noise does not significantly impact theta activity in the same way as changing-state speech, suggesting it does not interfere with working memory processes to the same extent.
findings.quote: which is not the case for the noise condition.

findings.antecedent: Irrelevant speech (Japanese narration) during visual digit presentation
findings.consequent: Gamma activity (20-80 Hz) at frontal clusters
findings.quote: a considerable increase in gamma (20-80 Hz) was identifiable for speech and noise at ~300-400 ms, but it did not differentiate between these two conditions

findings.antecedent: Continuous white noise during visual digit presentation
findings.consequent: Gamma activity (20-80 Hz) at frontal clusters
findings.quote: a considerable increase in gamma (20-80 Hz) was identifiable for speech and noise at ~300-400 ms, but it did not differentiate between these two conditions

mechanisms: Irrelevant speech automatically captures attentional resources, impairing the processing of visually presented items.
Reduced theta activity reflects a withdrawal of attentional resources from to-be-remembered items, impacting working memory.
Interference with the phonological loop (Baddeley's model).
Disruption of order information by coexisting order information from changing-state irrelevant sound (Jones' O-OER model).
Reduction of overall available attentional resources (Neath's feature model).
implementation_implications: The findings suggest that environments with changing-state irrelevant speech can detrimentally affect cognitive performance by reducing attentional resources and impairing working memory processes, even when the sound is not task-related and subjects are told to ignore it.
limitations: The study cannot claim with certainty whether the observed loss of sensory feature representations due to irrelevant sound is behaviorally relevant.

The study did not include a changing-state non-speech condition, which would be useful to clarify whether irrelevant speech affects different aspects of ERP or oscillatory activity compared to changing-state non-speech sounds.

A general problem arises when relating cognitive ISE models with neuroscientific approaches, as abstract concepts like 'modality-dependent information' are difficult to specify on a neurophysiological level.
